To proscribe something means to officially forbid it — to declare that it is not allowed and must not happen.

Think of it as a powerful, formal "NO" issued by someone or something with authority — a government, a law, an institution, a religion. When something is proscribed, it isn't just frowned upon or discouraged. It is actively and formally banned.

This is what separates proscribe from a simple word like "forbid." Proscribing always involves an official or authoritative act. You don't proscribe your friend from borrowing your pen. But a government can proscribe a dangerous chemical. A religion can proscribe certain behaviors. A professional body can proscribe a harmful medical practice.

The word carries the weight of official condemnation and prohibition.

Almost anything can be proscribed — actions, substances, practices, books, organizations, or groups. Here are realistic examples across different contexts:

Law & Government:

  • A government may proscribe terrorist organizations, meaning those groups are legally banned and any involvement with them is a criminal offense.
  • A country might proscribe the use of certain pesticides that are harmful to public health.

Religion & Culture:

  • Many religions proscribe certain foods, behaviors, or rituals — declaring them forbidden to followers.
  • Historically, certain books were proscribed by religious institutions and banned from being read or distributed.

Professional & Institutional:

  • Medical ethics boards can proscribe specific procedures that are deemed unsafe or unethical.
  • A school may proscribe the use of phones during examinations.
The Crucial Distinction: Proscribe vs. Prescribe

This is the single most important thing to lock in, because these two words look almost identical but mean opposite things.

  • Prescribe = to officially order or direct that something should be done.
    (A doctor prescribes medicine → they are telling you to take it.)
  • Proscribe = to officially order that something must not be done.
    (A law proscribes a substance → it is telling you it is forbidden.)

One simple way to remember: Prescribe = positive direction. Proscribe = prohibition.

If you're ever unsure in the moment, ask yourself: is the authority recommending/ordering action, or banning something? If it's a ban, it's proscribe.

Proscribing is not mild. It sits at the strong end of the spectrum of restriction:

  • Discourage → weak, advisory
  • Prohibit / forbid → clear ban
  • Proscribe → a formal, official, often legal or institutional ban, sometimes with stated consequences for violation

When something is proscribed, there is usually a system behind the ban — rules, enforcement, consequences.

In some contexts — especially in law — you can proscribe not just things or actions but organizations or groups. This means they are officially declared illegal and outlawed. In the UK, for example, terrorist groups are formally proscribed organizations under anti-terror legislation. Being a member of, supporting, or funding such a group then becomes a crime.

• "The treaty proscribes the development of biological weapons by any signatory nation."
  • "The cult was proscribed by the government after evidence of widespread abuse emerged."
  • "The new health regulations proscribe the addition of trans fats to any packaged food."
  • "Several ancient texts were proscribed by the church and ordered to be destroyed."
  • "The professional code of conduct explicitly proscribes any financial relationship between a therapist and their patient."
To proscribe something is to officially and authoritatively ban it — declaring it forbidden, often with consequences for those who defy the ban.
